ethics_check.report:
Based on the following text, we would expect an ethics approval statement, and it was present:

> All participants were born in Spain and claimed Spanish as their native language, except for two participants who reported Basque as their first language but learned Spanish before the age of 6 years (refer to Supplementary Tables A and B for the individual demographic data of the participants in the aphasia and control group, respectively).

> Two key differences between the Cinderella and the Hare and Tortoise story retells are that the former provides significantly less visual support, considering participants are asked to narrate the story just after viewing the pictures.

> Plausibly, when participants are involved in a single-picture description task, they first retrieve a frame structure that pre-activates the employment of relative clauses, facilitating the specification of nouns leading to a more informative description of the stimuli.

> Likewise, when participants are required to retell a story, they retrieve a frame structure that eases the availability of left branching clauses, which function as adjectival or adverbial phrases.

> Participants were also tested on a storytelling task in which they were required to narrate the story described in a sequence of pictures that were not made available during production.

power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: Statistical analyses were performed using Jamovi (v 2.3.21.0; 2023), and plots were obtained in R (version 4.2.3, R Core team, 2023) via the ggplot2 package (v 3.5.1; Wickham, 2016) from RStudio (R Core Team, 2023). For each group, measures of central tendency were first calculated for each task and dependent variable (see Tables 3 and 4). Afterwards, based on the parametricity of the data (obtained via Levene's Test for Homogeneity of Variances), either Kruskall-Wallis tests or Welch's One-Way ANOVAs were executed in order to compare syntactic and morphological variables between both groups in each task. P-values resulting from group comparisons for each variable within each task were corrected using the Benjamini-Hochberg method (Benjamini & Hochberg, 1995). Post hoc analyses were conducted after significant main effects of group were observed. A simulation-based post-hoc sensitivity power analysis was conducted in R using the PMCMRplus package (Pohlert, 2024) to estimate the minimum effect size our design had 80% power to detect at  = .05 (5000 simulations). We assessed the statistical power of each between-group comparison using the same parametric and non-parametric inferential tests as those used in the main analyses. Moreover, to characterize the empirical precision achieved by our study, we calculated effect-size estimates and their 95% confidence intervals (Appendix Table B) using the effect size package in R (Ben-Schachar et al. 2020).

Statistical sensitivity. The simulation-based sensitivity analysis indicated that the study had 80% power at α = .05 to detect standardized effects of approximately |d| = 1.10 for the Welch tests and |δ| = 0.50 for the Kruskall-Wallis tests. Thus, the study was primarily sensitive to large between-group effects, although effects smaller than these thresholds could also reach statistical significance in the observed sample. A full report of the effect size estimates and their 95% confidence intervals can be found in Appendix B.

Two key differences between the Cinderella and the Hare and Tortoise story retells are that the former provides significantly less visual support, considering participants are asked to narrate the story just after viewing the pictures.

Plausibly, when participants are involved in a single-picture description task, they first retrieve a frame structure that pre-activates the employment of relative clauses, facilitating the specification of nouns leading to a more informative description of the stimuli.
Likewise, when participants are required to retell a story, they retrieve a frame structure that eases the availability of left branching clauses, which function as adjectival or adverbial phrases.
Participants were also tested on a storytelling task in which they were required to narrate the story described in a sequence of pictures that were not made available during production.

text.text: Purpose: The aim of this study is to determine which of four tasks testing different discourse genres (descriptive, procedural, conversational, and narrative) is the most sensitive in detecting syntactic and morphological complexity deficits in Spanish aphasia.
Additionally, we compare two approaches for measuring syntax in discourse to identify the most accurate set of metrics for discriminating group membership.
Method: In this comparative cross-sectional study, we analyzed the discourse of an aphasia group (N = 20) and a non-brain-damaged group (N = 14).
Data was preprocessed using manual and automated procedures.
We measured syntactic complexity through proxies (mean length of utterance, noun-verb ratio, and verbs per utterance), in addition to a competing 'syntactic structures' metric.
The latter includes variables of subordination, left branching, relative clauses, and word integration, while morphological complexity was measured through an inflectional index.
Results: The descriptive and narrative tasks highlighted the most significant differences across syntactic complexity metrics between the groups.
Additionally, nested binomial logistic regression models showed that the 'syntactic structures' metric predicted groups better than the proxies alone.
Conclusions: A comprehensive assessment of syntactic complexity can be obtained through the administration of both descriptive and narrative tasks.
The measurement of 'syntactic structures' in discourse proved a fitter and finer-grained approach for group discrimination than the incorporation of syntactic proxies alone.
These findings provide guidance for a precise discourse assessment in Spanish aphasia.

Syntax and morphology -the rules governing sentence structure and word formation and inflection, respectively -are key language components that are often impaired in aphasia following damage to fronto-temporal regions of the left hemisphere and the white-matter fibers that connect them.

Syntactic complexity involves the use of recursive structures through clausal subordination and embedding (Hunt, 1970), while morphological complexity concerns how morphemes combine within words as well as how words relate to one another through inflection and derivation (Stump & Finkel, 2015).

text.text: To fill these gaps and guide researchers and clinicians toward a more efficient assessment of morphosyntactic deficits in aphasic discourse, this study investigates the simplification of syntactic and morphological complexity associated with aphasia in Spanish speakers, employing two metric approaches across different discourse genres to identify the most sensitive tasks and metrics.

Simplification of syntactic complexity, mainly manifested in a reduction of clause length and lower frequency of embedded clauses (Ulatowska et al., 1990), is a hallmark of impaired speech in speakers with aphasia (Schnur & Wang, 2024), especially those presenting with agrammatism, a cluster of language symptoms characterized by dysfunction in the production and comprehension of grammatical morphology and sentence structure (Menn & Obler, 1990).

text.text: While syntactic simplification has been a common discourse marker in aphasia research, comparing results proves challenging given that discourse metrics measuring syntactic complexity are highly variable as well (Armstrong, 2000; Linnik et al., 2015).

text.text: Two main approaches for measuring syntactic complexity can be discerned in aphasia studies.
The most traditional approach requires parsing each separate utterance, counting of embeddings, and considering the subordination characteristics.

Examples akin to direct measures of syntactic complexity include Glosser and Deser's (1991) 'weighted index of subordination', Sherratt's examination (2007) of subordinate clause frequency, clauses length, and the percentages of left branching, right branching, and main clauses; Wright and Capilouto's (2012) 'complexity index', and the automated extraction of 'syntactic accuracy' and 'structural complexity' scores reported by Schnur and Wang (2024).

text.text: Evaluating the frequency and type of subordination and embeddings provides a direct index of the integrity of speakers' syntactic representations and mechanisms, at the cost of complex and time-consuming discourse processing steps.
Another possible approach to measuring syntactic complexity is implementing syntactic proxies, which involves adopting indirect measures to represent the complexity of a speakers' syntax.

For instance, Vermeulen and colleagues (1989) described syntactic simplification in aphasic speech through reduced use of function words and shorter Mean Length of Utterance (MLU). Stark (2019) reported reduced proportion of verbs per utterance, in addition to an augmented noun-verb ratio and open-closed word class ratio.

text.text: The usage of syntactic proxies has the advantages of saving time and effort, since they allow for the automated extraction of such variables using discourse analysis programs.
Yet, metric analysis (e.g., the proportion of verbs per utterance or MLU) can only indirectly inform on finer-grained syntactic aspects, such as the presence of subordination and embeddings.

Relevant for this research, Agmon and colleagues (2024) proposed the 'syntactic structures' multidimensional metric, which consisted of cognitively demanding grammatical variables that are sensitive to aging or dementia.

text.text: Such metric considers subordination, a homologue to previously used embedding indexes (Bastiaanse et al., 1996a; Gordon, 2020; Schnur & Wang, 2024; Sherrat, 2007; Ulatowska et al., 1990; Wright & Capilouto, 2012); Relative clauses, i.e. a form of subordination where a dependent clause modifies a noun in the independent clause; Left-branching clauses, which refers to a special form of subordination where the embedded clause is placed before or within the main clause; and complex noun phrases and complex adjectival modifications, both representing intraclausal combinatorial syntactic phenomena (see Table 2 for illustrative examples). Agmon et al. text.text: An early focus of aphasia discourse studies was on the differential effects that elicitation genres had on linguistic measures.

Since the 1972 introduction of the Cookie Theft picture description task in the Boston Diagnostic Aphasia Exam (BDAE; Goodglass & Kaplan, 1972), different discourse elicitation methods have proliferated in both research and clinical assessment.

text.text: This has spurred increasing interest in whether discourse and associated metrics vary by task, and whether tasks can be meaningfully grouped into broader categories, such as discourse genres, based on the patterns they elicit, with potential clinical implications for the selection of assessment tools. Ulatowska and colleagues (1990) were among the first to demonstrate that different discourse genres tax the cognitive system distinctively and consequently elicit content that differs in information and structure (see also Doyle et al., 1995; Olness, 2006; Van Leer & Turkstra, 1999 for similar results).

text.text: The literature has converged on four core elicitation genres (Ulatowska et al., 1990; for a review, Bryant et al., 2016): expositional/descriptive, procedural/script, narrative, and conversational.

text.text: In the expositional genre, subjects describe a topic -usually prompted by a single image or picture sequence -whereas the procedural genre elicits explanations of how a particular activity is carried out.

The narrative genre involves recounting a factual or fictional story with characters, a setting, and a sequence of events, while the conversational genre entails an interactive dialogue with another speaker.

These four genres have been systematically operationalized in AphasiaBank (MacWhinney et al., 2011; MacWhinney, 2019), a computerized database of clinician-patient interviews built around a tightly specified elicitation protocol in which investigators follow a structured script for questioning and narrative elicitation.

text.text: A key advantage of AphasiaBank is its integration with the CHAT and CLAN programs, which allow a wide range of syntax-related indices to be computed automatically and accurately, facilitating cross-genre comparisons.

Recently, leveraging large-scale data from AphasiaBank and its computational resources, Stark (2019) systematically showed that expositional, narrative and procedural discourse each elicits unique linguistic features in both PWA and non-brain-damaged individuals. Stark and Fukuyama (2020) further highlighted that linguistic production is influenced by task type, aphasia type, and severity, with tasks in the same genre differing significantly from each other, while maintaining comparable linguistic features when compared to other genres.

text.text: Given the task-specific nature of discourse and the heterogeneity of aphasia, a comprehensive study comparing multiple genres within a unified protocol and a same sample is needed.

text.text: This articulate inflection paradigm renders subject pronouns pragmatically optional, classifying Spanish as a pro-drop language.
Verb phrases are structured around a lexical verb that may be accompanied by auxiliaries and clitic pronouns (El líbro loclitic leí ayer, 'The book, (I) read it yesterday').

The auxiliary haber constructs compound tenses followed by the past participle (he comido, '(I) have eaten'), while transitive verbs allow passive constructions formed with ser plus the past participle.
Spanish also offers several periphrastic constructions for temporal reference, most productively the present progressive (estar + gerund) and future-referring periphrases (ir a + infinitive).
Temporal adverbs such as ayer ('yesterday') and mañana ('tomorrow') must be compatible with the verb form used; any mismatch results in ungrammaticality (*ayer vendremos, 'yesterday we will come').

As for subordination, in Spanish complement clauses and relative clauses are syntactically fixed in post-head position (Creo que Juan llegó tarde, 'I think that Juan arrived late'; el libro que compré ayer, 'the book that I bought yesterday') (Real Academia Española, 2009).

text.text: Adverbial clauses, by contrast, are positionally flexible: while they most frequently appear post-verbally (Me quedé en casa porque llovía, 'I stayed home because it was raining'), they can be fronted for discourse-pragmatic reasons (Si llueve, me quedo en casa, 'If it rains, I'll stay home').
Investigations on the morphological complexity of aphasic discourse in Spanish are very scarce.

Using semi-structured interviews, Martínez-Ferreiro and colleagues (2017) investigated the production of verbal inflection in Spanish and reported a reduced rate of finite verbs produced by non-fluent people with mixed aphasia (PWA) compared to fluent PWA and the control group.

Greater information on finite verb production can be gathered from studies focusing on agrammatic production with structured tasks (e.g., delayed repetition, sentence completion, morphological transformation), which have generally reported selective impairment for tense compared to subject-verb agreement markers (person and number) (Benedet et al. 1998; Díeguez-Vide et al. 2012; Gavarró & Martínez-Ferreiro, 2007; Martínez-Ferreiro, 2003 , 2010 , 2013; Moreno-Torres Sánchez et al. 2005; Stecher et al. 2024; for a review, see Martínez-Ferreiro et al. 2015).

Available evidence on the syntactic complexity of speech in Spanish aphasia is also scarce.
Hernández-Sacristán and Rosell-Clarí (2009) investigated how a group of PWA utilized the Spanish and Catalan "que" (that) during natural, undirected conversation.

The results revealed not only that PWA used a restricted and simpler range of syntactic configurations compared to healthy controls (e.g., fewer relative clauses), but also that their speech was remarkably free of strictly ungrammatical errors.

Similarly, Martínez-Ferreiro et al. (2017) reported that the production of subordinate clauses by fluent and non-fluent PWA in semi-structured interviews was significantly lower compared to a group of unimpaired speakers, although the study does not indicate the type of subordinate clauses produced.

text.text: Taken together, these findings from studies testing agrammatic and mixed-aphasia speakers suggest that syntactic and morphological complexity are reduced in Spanish aphasic discourse, with structured task settings confirming significant impairment in terms of inflection and subordinate clause production.

The current study aims to investigate how discourse tasks of different elicitation genres capture syntactic simplification and morphological deficits associated with aphasia in Spanish speakers.
Our goals and approach are motivated by the clinical and research relevance of ecologically valid methods for the evaluation of clinical populations (Davidson et al., 2003; WHO, 2018).
text.formatted: Our goals and approach are motivated by the clinical and research relevance of ecologically valid methods for the evaluation of clinical populations <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Davidson et al., 2003;</ref> <ref type="bibr">WHO, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: As reviewed above, spoken language can be elicited through a variety of discourse methods, each placing different demands on speakers that, in turn, can give rise to task-specific degrees of morphological and syntactic complexity in the output.

In a similar vein, a range of syntactic complexity measures can be extracted from spontaneous speech, with their relative frequency shaped by the type of task used, presumably due to top-down adjustments in the task-specific conceptual frames generated during the early stages of discourse production (Sherratt, 2007).

text.text: Comparing outcomes across discourse genres and identifying which metrics and tasks best capture syntactic complexity in Spanish can support the adoption of ecologically valid methods in both research and clinical settings.
Critically, by examining discourse production in Spanish, our study also aims to enrich the field of aphasiology by contributing data from an underrepresented language.
Hence, we attempt to answer three main questions: (1) Which discourse task is more sensitive to the detection of syntactic complexity simplification in the discourse of Spanish PWA?
(2) Which discourse task is more sensitive to the detection of morphological complexity deficits?
(3) Is 'syntactic structures' metric (Agmon et al., 2024) a better fit for assessing aphasic features in connected speech than the syntactic proxies one?

text.text: Identifying the most suitable metrics and elicitation tasks to detect syntactic and morphological impairment has the potential to inform therapeutic programs (Leaman & Edmonds, 2023) and supports the crosslinguistic goal of disentangling language-specific impairments in Spanish aphasia (Linnik et al., 2015).

text.text: Although comparison between narrative and conversational genres are uncommon, the dialogic nature of conversational discourse allows for less conventional grammar to emerge in produced utterances (Armstrong et al., 2011; Beeke et al., 2003; Sajjadi et al., 2012).

text.text: Thus, we hypothesize that a narrative task will be the most sensitive in detecting syntactic complexity deficits.

Considering the possibility of eliciting more verbs with person and tense inflections, (Olness, 2006; Stark & Fukuyama, 2020), we hypothesize that the narrative task will also be the most sensitive in detecting morphological complexity deficits.

text.text: In order to examine whether the syntactic proxies or the 'syntactic structures' metric better predicted group category, four binomial logistic regression models were implemented using all discourse samples combined.
Differently from Agmon and colleagues (2024), we used a nested modelling approach, which allowed for an accurate statistical comparison of the amount of variance explained by each model.

Predictive performance was assessed using several key measures: accuracy, which refers to the proportion of both correct positive and negative predictions out of total predictions; sensitivity (i.e. the proportion of actual positives correctly identified), specificity (i.e. the proportion of actual negatives correctly identified), and the Area Under the Curve (AUC), which provides an overall assessment of the model's ability to discriminate between groups.
For this matter, 3 nested models were designed progressively including: A.1) the syntactic proxies, A.2) the measures contained in the 'syntactic structures', and A.3) the error-centered variables.

A fourth model (B) was implemented after trimming for the predictors that showed high collinearity (i.e., a Variance Inflation Factors [VIF] greater than 5), and was based on its significant contribution to model fitness, to enhance parsimony.

The current study aimed to identify which elicitation methods, from a set of tasks pertaining to different discourse genres, were most sensitive to capturing simplification of syntactic and morphological complexity in Spanish aphasia, and to determine the best measurement approach for this purpose.

PWA and control participants' speech was analyzed to quantify syntactic proxies, such as mean length of utterance, number of verbs per utterance, noun-verb ratio; syntactic structure variables, which included different types of subordinate clauses (relative, left-branching clauses), complex noun phrases and adjectival/adverbial modifications; and finally, error-centered variables (i.e., ungrammatical sentences and morphological errors).
The performance of these different metrics was compared to assess their accuracy in classifying participants into either PWA or control participants.

Based on previous studies (Olness, 2006; Schnur & Wang, 2024; Stark, 2019; Stark & Fukuyama, 2020; Ulatowska et al., 1981; Ulatowska et al., 1990), we hypothesized that the narrative task would elicit the most significant differences between the aphasia and control group in both syntactic and morphological complexity, and that syntactic structure variables would be more accurate than proxies in determining participants' group membership, in line with Agmon et al. (2024).

(2024)</ref>.

text.text: The results only partially support our hypotheses.
Both the descriptive and the narrative tasks were useful to identify patterns of syntactic simplification, although to differing degrees.
Moreover, none of the four tasks elicited significant group differences in morphological complexity.
Finally, fine-grained syntactic structure metrics proved to be fitter and more accurate than proxies in determining group membership.
In the following, we discuss these results and their implications in greater detail.

Analyses of variance indicates both the Cookie Theft picture description and the Hare and the Tortoise story retell tasks were sensitive to detecting syntactic simplification in aphasic speech, although the scope of their sensitivity appears to differ.

On one hand, the Cookie Theft picture description consistently and reliably elicited group differences in several dependent variables that included both syntactic proxies and syntactic structure, such as MLU, relative and subordinate clauses and complex noun phrases and adjectival modification, but not in error-related measures.
On the other hand, the Hare and Tortoise study retell showed reliable group differences in left branching and complex adjectival/adverbial modification.

Moreover, our PWA group tended to produce a significantly higher number of ungrammatical sentences compared to the control group (although this effect sits slightly below the minimum detectable effect threshold indicated by our sensitivity analysis, see Appendix B).

Overall, these results are at odds with our research hypothesis, which stated that the narrative genre-Hare and Tortoise story retell-would be the most sensitive to detecting syntactic complexity deficits in PWA.

Based on previous findings (Schnur & Wang, 2024), we expected that the narrative task would elicit more syntactically complex discourse than the descriptive task in aphasic populations, which would in turn be reflected in greater inter-group differences.

text.text: Two key differences between the Cinderella and the Hare and Tortoise story retells are that the former provides significantly less visual support, considering participants are asked to narrate the story just after viewing the pictures.
In contrast, in the Hare and Tortoise task speakers can inspect the four-picture material while narrating the story.

Furthermore, it is possible that the Cinderella story retell elicits syntactically more complex content, as its narrative involves a longer plot, and a greater number of characters and constituent events compared to our task.
Overall, our data show that descriptive and narrative tasks may be sensitive to group differences at different syntactic levels.

On the one hand, the Hare and Tortoise story retell task elicits reliable group differences in the number of subordinate clauses, left branching and adjectival/adverbial modifications, all of which relate to speakers' capacity to build hierarchically structured sentences through clause-level modifications.

On the other hand, the Cookie Theft picture description task is able to detect group differences in syntactic complexity also at the NPlevel, as evidenced by the significant difference between the two groups in relative clauses and complex NPs.

Plausibly, picture description tasks require speakers to introduce NPs associated with referents identified in a visually rich scene and to elaborate on them through devices such as relative clauses, while narrating a story demands the creation of a temporal and causal scaffolding that relies more on left branching and adjectival/adverbial modifications.
Visual inspection of the data (Figure 2) seems to corroborate this interpretation.
text.formatted: Visual inspection of the data (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_4">2</ref>) seems to corroborate this interpretation.

text.text: Specifically, describing a picture and narrating a story may lead the control group to preferentially produce NP-or clause-level syntactic complexity, respectively.

Although our narrative task showed less consistency in demonstrating significant group differences across syntactic variables than the Cookie Theft picture description, when comparing both tasks within the control group (see exploratory analysis in the Supplementary Table S6) significant differences (before Benjamini-Hochberg correction) show that the Hare and the Tortoise story retell evoked longer left-branching clauses and more complex adjectival/adverbial modifications than the Cookie Theft description task.

text.text: Specifically, left branching clauses were frequently used as adjectival/adverbial phrases, since they provided supplementary information pertaining to various aspects such as time specifications, cause-and-effect relationships, and conditional statements.
In contrast, a greater number of relative clauses was produced in the Cookie Theft picture description compared to the Hare and Tortoise task.

The increased frequency of relative clauses boosted the mean dependency distance in relative clauses and amplified the number of words in complex noun phrases (see for example participant 23 in Table 2).
text.formatted: The increased frequency of relative clauses boosted the mean dependency distance in relative clauses and amplified the number of words in complex noun phrases (see for example participant 23 in Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_1">2</ref>).

text.text: While these patterns should be confirmed by further studies with larger samples, they suggest that speakers within the control group tended to employ a different pattern of syntactic structures and discursive resources in order to respond to the particularities of each task demand, in line with Sherrat's (2007) model.

Plausibly, when participants are involved in a single-picture description task, they first retrieve a frame structure that pre-activates the employment of relative clauses, facilitating the specification of nouns leading to a more informative description of the stimuli.
Likewise, when participants are required to retell a story, they retrieve a frame structure that eases the availability of left branching clauses, which function as adjectival or adverbial phrases.

Adverbial clauses are desirable for a narrative task given they provide an explicit organizing scaffold to a sequence of events, while left branching clauses can operate as a stylistic device that builds up suspense.
However, additional research is necessary to corroborate this interpretation and clarify the specific task properties that influence the use of complex syntactic structures.

In line with Ulatowska et al. (1990), the Hare and the Tortoise story retell not only elicited significant differences between groups in MLU and most 'syntactic structure' variables, but also in the proportion of ungrammatical utterances, unlike the Cookie Theft picture description.

(1990)</ref>, the Hare and the Tortoise story retell not only elicited significant differences between groups in MLU and most 'syntactic structure' variables, but also in the proportion of ungrammatical utterances, unlike the Cookie Theft picture description.

text.text: Narrating a story involves the embedding of its events in a temporal scaffold and thus it can trigger the formulation of tense sequences and richer syntactic structures, which in turn can increase the probability of producing ungrammatical structures.
Eliciting ungrammatical utterances in aphasia assessment has great clinical value, since it can provide qualitative information about which specific language mechanisms are impaired.

The present results also align with prior literature identifying procedural (Stark, 2019; Stark & Fukuyama, 2020; Ulatowska et al., 1981) and conversational genres (Armstrong et al., 2011; Beeke et al., 2003; Sajjadi et al., 2012) as unfit elicitation methods for the assessment of syntax.

text.text: The Ham and Cheese Sandwich procedural task evoked a high noun-verb ratio given the frequent list-like utterances employed, and the fewest number of utterances (e.g., participant 22: "you need sliced bread, ham, cheese and butter" ["se necesitan pan de molde, jamón, queso y mantequilla"]).

In contrast, the Structured Interview conversational task elicited the largest number of utterances prompted by five consecutive questions, but the outcome of both groups was often syntactically poor and short in length.
This conversational task did not demand extensive answers, as the syntactic information contained in the questions themselves allowed for pragmatically short responses.
As an illustration, participant 33 of the control group briefly responded to the question "What are you going to do for Christmas?"
("¿qué va a hacer en Navidades?") with "spending time with the family" ("hacer vida en familia [% cn:3]").
Although in line with previous literature, our failure to detect syntactic complexity in these two tasks should be interpreted with caution, given their limited power (Appendix B).

Beyond the constraints imposed by sample size, the reduced power observed in these two tasks may nevertheless reflect the nature of the speech they elicited: both the list-like formulaic utterances and the pragmatically short responses of the structured-interview task offered very few opportunities for most of the syntactic structure variables under investigation to occur.

This restricted range not only limits the number of observable target structures per participant but may also mean that group differences in syntactic capacity are less likely to be elicited by these two tasks, in contrast to the greater variety of syntactic structures available in narrative and descriptive elicitation contexts.
Furthermore, we consider that both pragmatic and contextual factors influenced the performance of participants in the discourse tasks.

An important consideration is that participants' informativeness and engagement, as evidenced by the length and number of utterances, may be significantly influenced not only by clinical variables but also by the assessment setting, session rapport, and their inherent personality traits.
This is especially relevant for the Structured Interview, where questions delve into the speakers' personal lives and habits.

Consequently, in addition to syntactic impairment, the high variability in the number of utterances observed in the Structured Interview (see Table 3) may also be explained by differences in expressive pragmatic skills and/or individual and situational differences (Armstrong et al., 2011).

Morphological complexity was assessed using the inflectional index, which divided the number of correctly inflected words by the total number of inflected words.

Overall, morphological errors were uncommon (a frequency similar to that reported by Stark and Fukuyama, 2020), with the aphasia group making three times as many (n = 30) as the control group (n = 9).

text.text: The low frequency of errors led to the inflectional index being non-robust, as it neither showed significant group differences in any discourse task in the analysis of variance, nor did it predict group membership in the binomial logistic regression.

However, a trend was observed in the Structured Interview, consistent with findings from Sajjadi et al. (2012), where a task effect in the inflectional index reached significance before correcting for multiple comparisons (Table 5).

text.text: This result, contrary to our research hypothesis, may be partly explained by the design of the questions, which are intended to elicit verbs in various tense-mood inflections, potentially increasing the opportunities for inflectional errors to surface.

However, participants often opted for non-finite verbal forms instead of the target tensed forms, which may have attenuated group differences and could account for why the effect did not survive correction for multiple comparisons.

Additionally, this task is cognitively demanding, as it prompts extended discourse through novel questions that require participants to respond via retrieving coherent episodes from long-term memory (Bliss & McCabe, 2006).

text.text: The present results indicate that 'syntactic structures' provide a model with good fitness and discriminatory power when predicting aphasia versus control groups.
Crucially, its fitness and predictive power is not affected when excluding syntactic proxies such as MLU and verbs per utterance, which were found to be collinear with syntactic structure variables.
Notably, the model is significantly enhanced in discriminative ability and fitness when error-centered variables are included.
This suggests that including predictors that measure morphological and grammatical errors is relevant, as these variables indicate difficulties in computing morphosyntactic relations.
Word-and utterance-level errors, characteristic of the discourse of speakers with aphasia, are frequently assessed in current aphasiology research and clinical practices (Stark et al., 2021b).

text.text: Thus, it is appropriate that these linguistic phenomena are noted when designing a model that is discriminative between aphasic and non-brain damage discourse.
Recent accounts of morphosyntactic impairments in post-stroke aphasia have advocated for the processing, rather than structural, nature of the deficit.

From this perspective, difficulties in the production (and comprehension) of verb inflection and of different types of structures do not stem from the loss of underlying syntactic representations (Tree Pruning Hypothesis, Friedman & Grodzinsky, 1997; Trace Deletion Hypothesis, Grodzinsky, 1995; see Druks, 2016 for a review), but from the damage to specific processing mechanisms (Kolk & Heeschen, 1992; Kok et al. 2007; McNeil et al., 1994; Thompson, 2003, to name a few; see a review in Bastiaanse & Thompson, 2012).
text.formatted: From this perspective, difficulties in the production (and comprehension) of verb inflection and of different types of structures do not stem from the loss of underlying syntactic representations (Tree Pruning Hypothesis, Friedman & Grodzinsky, 1997; Trace Deletion Hypothesis, <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">Grodzinsky, 1995;</ref> <ref type="bibr">see Druks, 2016</ref> for a review), but from the damage to specific processing mechanisms <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">(Kolk & Heeschen, 1992;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">Kok et al. 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">McNeil et al., 1994;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b103">Thompson, 2003</ref>, to name a few; see a review in <ref type="bibr">Bastiaanse & Thompson, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Our approach and findings are agnostic to both structural and processing accounts, in that we limit our investigation to metrics that best detect morphosyntactic simplification to predict group membership.

However, the different degrees of syntactic simplification that we observe within our PWA group are more easily accounted for under a processing account, since variability in performance is not compatible with the assumption that syntactic representations are unavailable to aphasic speakers.

The lack of online dependent variables, structured stimuli and instructions, and specific experimental manipulations, combined with recruitment criteria that extend beyond agrammatic patients, prevent us from pinpointing the precise syntactic processing mechanisms that may be impaired.

Our finding that regression models including hierarchical syntactic measures are more accurate at classifying speakers with and without aphasia could, however, provide some hints about the levels of linguistic analysis at which impaired mechanisms could operate.
Specifically, it suggests that in our sample of PWA, the impairment goes beyond the lexical level, reaching processing stages involved in e.g., syntactic structure planning and building.
In this respect, two specific patterns are worth highlighting.

First, the reduced proportion of left-branching structures, which may require the speaker to hold complex material in memory before reaching the head of the sentence, could reflect impairment in sentence planning mechanisms (arguably mediated by short-term and working memory deficits).
Such impairments can be probed with dedicated tasks (Lee et al. 2015; Van Boxtel et al. 2023) and through the analysis of speech dysfluencies, though this falls beyond the scope of the present study.

text.text: Second, the significant contribution of ungrammatical sentence proportion opens a window onto the integrity of monitoring mechanisms (Botvinick et al. 2001), i.e., the speaker's ability to detect and repair errors.

text.text: While theoretically plausible, these implications remain tentative and should be corroborated by data from structured linguistic and cognitive tasks collected in larger samples.
Despite being limited to behavioral data, this study carries meaningful implications for the brain-language relationship, which future research could further investigate.

Specifically, the present results suggest that the heterogeneous brain damage in our sample, which resulted in aphasia, may have affected resources needed to necessary to successfully deploy complex syntactic structures, such as left-branching clauses and relative clauses (see Den Ouden et al., 2008 , Kirchner et al. 2018 and Lorca-Puls, 2024 for evidence regarding neuroanatomical correlates of complex syntax production and expressive agrammatism).

text.text: As noted earlier, these syntactic devices differ not only in their complexity, but also in their locality and function.
Relative clauses attach postnominally to an already established head, supporting local, within-sentence referential elaboration.
Left-branching clauses, by contrast, are preposed and require the speaker to build and hold open a hierarchical dependency before reaching the main clause.
Moreover, they typically encode temporal, causal and conditional relations that make up a discourse model.

Although mapping behavioral impairment to (lesioned) brain regions is clearly beyond the scope of this study, this functional distinction parallels proposals of a graded cortical hierarchy in which local, sentence-level combinatorial processing is supported by brain regions that operate over intermediate temporal integration windows, such as the superior temporal gyrus (Lerner et al. 2011).
text.formatted: Although mapping behavioral impairment to (lesioned) brain regions is clearly beyond the scope of this study, this functional distinction parallels proposals of a graded cortical hierarchy in which local, sentence-level combinatorial processing is supported by brain regions that operate over intermediate temporal integration windows, such as the superior temporal gyrus <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">(Lerner et al. 2011)</ref>.

text.text: In contrast, maintaining and updating a discourse model across sentences involves also regions with longer temporal receptive windows, such as temporo-parietal and prefrontal areas (Lerner et al. 2011; see also Catani and Bambini, 2014), with these two levels interfacing rather than operating as separate modules.

text.text: The present research addressed this need in the clinical field of Spanish aphasia by aiming to identify the most sensitive discourse tasks and metrics for eliciting and detecting syntactic and morphological complexity simplification.
Based on our findings, two methodological suggestions can be put forward for researchers and clinicians aiming to comprehensively assess syntactic complexity in Spanish speakers with aphasia.

Firstly, when evaluating syntactic complexity, it is pertinent to conjointly administer descriptive and narrative tasks, such as the Cookie Theft picture description (or an equivalent single-picture description task, e.g. the Picnic Scene from the Western Aphasia Battery; Kertesz, 2007) and a narrative task akin to our Hare and the Tortoise story retell.

text.text: This recommendation is supported by the reliable group differences elicited across several syntactic metrics by the descriptive task, the group difference in ungrammatical utterances elicited by the narrative task (a critical clinical marker of aphasia), and the distinct patterns of syntactic resources observed across tasks, consistent with Stark and Fukuyama's (2020) argument for the use of varied discourse elicitation methods for aphasia evaluation.

Secondly, from the obtained discourse samples, it is beneficial for researchers to measure a set of fit and noncollinear indicators such as noun-verb ratio, a broad embedding index (e.g., the employed subordination metric), dependency distances between the modifying verb within the relative clause and the relativized noun in the main clause, depth of left branching clauses, length of the complex noun phrases and adjectival/adverbial modifications, and proportion of ungrammatical utterances.
The obtained measures could then greatly inform research and clinical settings to guide rehabilitation procedures.
The most evident limitation of the current study is the small sample size, which limits statistical power such that only large effects can be reliably detected.

text.text: In brief, LARSP offers a descriptive taxonomy of syntactic production organized across three main levels of analysis: the word level, capturing morphological markers; the phrase level, examining the internal elaboration of noun, verb, and prepositional phrases; and the clause level, investigating how elements combine within the main clause.
These structures are analyzed with respect to developmental stages designed to identify the most natural next step in a patient's linguistic growth, thereby informing rehabilitation practices.
Although our work shares LARSP's commitment to multi-level structural analysis, the clinical focus on remediation and its stages clearly falls outside our scope.
In this sense, our quantitative approach extends the principled structural logic that LARSP established, without seeking to replace its clinical longitudinal insights.

Together, these factors prevented us from investigating and discussing genre effects on the morphological and syntactic complexity across different aphasia subtypes, severity and cognitive profiles, thus restricting our comparisons to the PWA vs. control group contrast.

Previous aphasiology research has found evidence for the simplification of both syntactic (Bastiaanse et al., 1996a; Glosser & Deser, 1991) and morphological complexity (Bastiaanse et al., 1996b; Bastiaanse et al., 2002; Martínez-Ferreiro et al., 2017) in fluent and nonfluent aphasia.

text.text: A larger, more controlled, sample could allow for testing the sensitivity and accuracy of our metrics across aphasia profiles and exploring possible interactions with tasks, an avenue we intend to pursue in future extensions of this work.

Nevertheless, this investigation represents an initial step toward validating the hierarchical syntactic structure metrics as tools for accurately detecting patterns of syntactic simplification in PWA and language-unimpaired speakers.
A second limitation of the present study is the failure to include covariates in the analyses due to heteroscedasticity in most variables, which required non-parametric tests.

Increasing the sample size is unlikely to resolve this issue, as the 'syntactic structures' metric showed frequent floor effects and a strongly left-skewed distribution, as anticipated by Agmon et al. (2024).

text.text: Likewise, the error-centered metrics faced similar challenges.

These limitations may be intrinsic to the 'syntactic structures' metric, as it does not account for elements essential to communication, allowing participants to complete tasks without using complex syntactic structures like relative or left-branching clauses.
A third limitation is the lack of reliability and stability estimates for the employed outcome variables.
Therefore, as the employed outcome variables lack standardization, it is uncertain to what degree each reflects the linguistic integrity of the participants.

Thus, future extensions of this study should investigate which syntactic and morphological discourse metrics are stable over time through test-retest studies with speakers with aphasia (Stark et al., 2021a).

text.text: A further limitation of the present study concerns the cross-linguistic generalizability of task-based findings.

Our results suggest that the narrative task was not more sensitive than the descriptive task in detecting syntactic complexity deficits in Spanish-speaking PWA, which contrasts with findings reported in English (Schnur & Wang, 2024; Stark, 2019; Stark & Fukuyama, 2020; Ulatowska et al., 1981; Ulatowska et al., 1990).

text.text: Moreover, the morphological properties of Spanish, such as the bound nature of verb stems, may constrain the type of errors and avoidance strategies available to PWA, which would in turn influence the sensitivity of the inflectional index.

However, the present study was not designed to directly compare task-elicited syntactic or morphological complexity across languages and therefore cannot determine whether this discrepancy is attributable to language-specific morphosyntactic properties of Spanish or to other methodological factors discussed above.

Future research should directly address these gaps by comparing task-elicited syntactic and morphological complexity across languages using equivalent tasks and metrics, in order to better understand how language-specific properties interact with discourse genre in shaping morphosyntactic production in both typical and aphasic populations.
Finally, the current study only employed an inflectional index (an accuracy indicator based on Bastiaanse et al., 1996b) as a measure of morphological complexity.

text.text: The results suggest that the inflectional index evokes exceedingly modest differences between the aphasia and control groups.

In order to have a better insight of task effects in verb production within aphasic discourse, future research should inspect the distribution of finite and non-finite forms (Martinez-Ferreiro et al., 2017), and implement a finer-grained analysis on the types of inflections, at the interface with other levels of language (Bastiaanse & Prins, 1994).

text.text: The current study showed that picture-based descriptive and narrative tasks are sensitive tools for the detection of syntactic simplification in the spontaneous speech of Spanish PWA, while the analysis of morphological integrity may require the combination of (dialogic) discourse with constrained tasks.
Fine-grained aspects of syntactic production, such as subordination, relative clauses and left-branching depth, emerge as highly accurate predictors of speakers' group membership.

In conclusion, this study highlights the combined utility of specific discourse tasks and structured metrics to reveal syntactic simplification in aphasia, underscoring the value of multi-dimensional assessments in comprehensively understanding language impairments.
